name: 農園直送レストラン 古都華 (Nouen Chokuso Restaurant Kotoka)

claims.text: The signature lunch comes with an all-you-can-eat buffet of seasonal Yamato vegetables, giving plant-forward diners a generous spread of fresh produce to build a meal from.
Ingredients are delivered direct from vetted prefecture farms, so the vegetable selection is fresh and seasonal.
The mains are mostly deep-fried wheat-breaded items (tonkatsu, tempura, fried chicken, fried fish, croquettes) sharing fryer oil, and no gluten-free accommodation is documented.
Obanzai sides and miso soup use standard Japanese seasonings (soy sauce, miso) that typically contain wheat; no wheat-free soy sauce is mentioned.
Vegetable obanzai are prepared in an omnivore kitchen alongside meat and fish and are likely seasoned with fish dashi; vegan separation is not documented.
The buffet-style choose-your-sides format makes it easy to build a vegetable-leaning plate, and an English menu helps with asking about ingredients.
Signature reicha is a powdered blend of 20-plus beans and grains plus green tea, which may contain or be cross-contaminated with wheat; no gluten-free handling is documented.
Headline cafe items (hojicha latte ice, strawberry-milk ice) are dairy-based and toppings include ice cream and mochi, so vegan separation is not assured.
Plain teas (Yamato tea, Taiwanese tea) are naturally plant-based options for vegan visitors.

name: おはなさんのおむすび屋さん (Ohana-san no Omusubi-yasan)

claims.text: Takeout offerings include homemade kombu and tsukudani, which are typically simmered in wheat-based soy sauce; soy sauce content is not declared gluten-free.
The set comes with grilled fish and the miso soup is made with morning dashi (not specified as kombu-only), so vegan separation is not assured.
Rice is the focus: Koshihikari from the Yamato Highlands, with onigiri formed gently to order, so plain salted or kombu onigiri may be requestable à la carte.
Okonomiyaki and modern-yaki are wheat-flour batter dishes cooked on a shared teppan; no gluten-free handling is documented.
Okonomiyaki sauce and dashi at Kansai griddle shops typically contain wheat; no allergen information is published for this shop.
Akashi-yaki is served in fish-based dashi and dishes rely on egg, pork, and seafood; no vegan preparation is documented.
An all-flour-based cake and pastry kitchen with no documented gluten-free items; not suitable for celiacs.
Cakes are dairy- and egg-based; no vegan options documented.

name: 御菓子司 萬勝堂 (Okashitsukasa Manshodo)

claims.text: Small traditional wagashi shop with a shared kitchen producing wheat-based cakes, manjū and dango alongside any wheat-free items; cross-contact with flour is likely and no allergen separation is documented.
Signature mitarashi dango is finished with a soy-sauce-based mitarashi glaze, which in standard form contains wheat.
Seasonal kakigōri includes a dairy (milk) version (Yamato-tea milk kintoki), prepared in the same small space as other items.

Several traditional items are naturally plant-based and wheat-free in concept (kuzukiri kudzu noodles, wasanbon rakugan, azuki-bean sweets), giving flexible diners some options if confirmed at the counter.

name: 御菓子司 鶴屋徳満 本店 (Okashitsukasa Tsuruya Tokuman Honten)

claims.text: The shop produces a wide range of wheat-based confections (castella, sponge-filled mikasa cakes, senbei, monaka wafers) in the same kitchen, so any naturally wheat-free item carries cross-contact risk; no gluten-free handling is documented.
Egg- and dairy-containing sweets such as castella and sponge-based mikasa are made alongside plant-based azuki, kuzu, and agar confections; no vegan-specific separation is documented.

The signature kakigori is described as shaved ice with house-made red bean paste and wasanbon-sugar/molasses syrup, and the 'Aoniyoshi' is made from kudzu starch and sugar — these particular items are plant-based and wheat-free by tradition, though they should still be confirmed for cross-contact and ingredients on site.
